title: Imaging superconducting weak spots through vortex-assisted THz near-field photovoltage
authors: Sergio J. Salvía-Fernández, Ekaterina Khestanova, Zoe Velluire-Pellat, Leonardo R. Cadorim, Sergi Batlle-Porro, David A. Czaplewski, Johann Osmond, Sebastian Castilla, Adrian Bachtold, Milorad V. Milošević, Aharon Kapitulnik, Frank H. L. Koppens
abstract: Nanoscale inhomogeneities are a defining feature of many superconducting materials, yet their local electromagnetic response has remained difficult to access experimentally. This is because their relevant energy scale lies in the terahertz range, where wavelengths -- on the order of hundreds of microns -- are too large to spatially resolve nanoscopic variations. Here, we demonstrate the first application of THz near-field photovoltage nanoscopy in a superconductor, achieving 300 nm spatial resolution at 2.52 THz. Scanning a current-biased NbN strip, we reveal photovoltage peaks within the bulk associated with nanoscopic defects of reduced superfluid density. The observed photovoltage follows the evolution of the vortex-dissipative state and is attributed to enhanced vortex-antivortex pair nucleation at defect sites. Together, these results open a direct route to probing how material inhomogeneities influence light-matter interactions in superconductors, with implications for superconducting devices and strongly inhomogeneous systems such as high-Tc and moiré materials.
summary: The research introduces THz near-field photovoltage nanoscopy to overcome the spatial resolution limits of traditional THz measurements in superconductors. By scanning a current-biased superconducting strip, the authors mapped localized photovoltage peaks that directly correlate with nanoscale material defects. This technique establishes a powerful new tool for investigating how disorder influences light-matter interactions and vortex dynamics in superconducting materials.
main_problem: The challenge is experimentally resolving nanoscale inhomogeneities (weak spots) within superconducting materials because their relevant energy scales are in the terahertz range, which far-field THz radiation cannot spatially resolve.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a technique to map these weak spots by observing localized photovoltage peaks associated with enhanced vortex-antivortex pair nucleation at material defects.
method: They employed THz near-field photovoltage nanoscopy using an AFM tip as a nanoantenna to locally probe the superconducting response while applying a DC bias current.
model_or_system: The experiment uses superconducting films, such as NbN strips, which exhibit nanoscale inhomogeneities. The physics is modeled by considering vortex dynamics and pair-breaking effects induced by the THz near-field excitation.
key_observables: Photovoltage peaks ($V_{PV}$), Full Width at Half Maximum ($	ext{FWHM}$) of the peak, and the dependence of $V_{PV}$ on bias current ($I_b$).
important_parameters: Spatial resolution ($\sim 300 	ext{ nm}$), THz frequency ($2.52 	ext{ THz}$), and superconducting gap energy scale.
main_assumptions: The observed photovoltage is attributed to enhanced vortex-antivortex pair nucleation at defect sites, which is supported by time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations.
figures_summary: Figures show local $V_{PV}$ peak maps varying with bias current and temperature, confirming localized peaks in the bulk due to defects. Comparisons are made between these measurements and DC transport characteristics ($	ext{d}V/	ext{d}I$).
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the limitations of far-field THz probing for nanoscale features. It then details the experimental setup, presenting results showing localized $V_{PV}$ peaks correlated with defects. Finally, it uses theoretical modeling (TDGL) to interpret the current and temperature dependence of these observed photovoltage signals.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, non-equilibrium optical probe into local superconducting order parameter suppression caused by material disorder, which is crucial for understanding high-Tc superconductors and moiré systems where inhomogeneity dominates physics.
